Zeta Zeta Chapter Hosts
Memorable Convention
The 138th Convention, held in the incomparably
beautiful city of Vancouver, British Columbia, from Au
gust nineteenth through August twenty-third, marked a
long anticipated first for Psi Upsilon. After waiting pa
tiently since its founding in 1935, the Zeta Zeta, our
illustrious twenty-ninth Chapter to be chartered, hosted
its first Convention. It proved to be well worth the fortysix-year wait. Some sixty-six official delegates and close to
one hundred and fifty others gathered on the University
of British Columbia's magnificent campus for four days of
serious business meetings and memorable social gather
ings.
Wednesday afternoon saw alumni and undergraduates
streaming in from far and wide to register at the newly
renovated Zeta Zeta Chapter House, before proceeding
to Walter Gage Residence, a splendid high-rise dormi
tory which became home for those in attendance. After a
buffet dinner at the House, an orientation meeting was
held at which Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, Executive Vice
President of the Fraternity, discussed expectations �
what the delegates might expect to gain from the Conven
tion and what the Convention expected from each of the
delegates. Regional Conferences followed, where under
graduates were given an opportunity to exchange ideas
and to discuss mutual concerns. Each day's activities
concluded with an open house at the Zeta Zeta Chapter
House, where good cheer and the spirit of brotherhood
were plentiful.
Thursday morning's business session was a very special
one for Psi Upsilon. It was a privilege to have as our guest
Mrs. Eileen Stevens, President of C.H.U.C.K. (Com
mittee to Halt Useless College Killings). Mrs. Stevens
gave a
stirring talk on the very controversial subject of
hazing, which was followed by a
lively discussion. Those
in attendance left the meeting with a
unique awareness of
the problem and a firm resolve to take the necessary steps
to eliminate it.
Edward E. Jefferys, Zeta Zeta '52, Convention Chair
man, was the able toastmaster for Thursday's opening
luncheon, at which George E. Price, Omega-Zeta Zeta
'59, Medical Director ofthe Health Sciences Center Hos
pital and Vice President of the Psi Upsilon Alumni Asso
ciation of British Columbia, delivered appropriate re
marks.
The 138th Convention of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity
officially convened Thursday afternoon. The meeting was
called to order by David S. McDiarmid, Zeta Zeta '64,
President ofthe Psi Upsilon Alumni Association of British
Columbia. After temporary officers were appointed, J.
Russell McShane, Delta '32, President of the Executive
Council, read the Annual Communication. The general
meeting was then adjourned so that the standing commit
tees could begin their deliberations on the pertinent
issues facing the Fraternity.
Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39 gives some "fatherly advice" to the
undergraduates at the orientation meeting on Wednesday
evening.

The summer meeting of the Executive Council, held
later that afternoon, provided an opportunity for all to
witness the governing body of the Fraternity in action. It
was followed by a salmon barbecue at the Zeta Zeta
House, a veritable feast for the parched and hungry dele
gates after the long day of business sessions.
On Friday business continued, with standing commit
tee meetings and a general meeting in the morning, and
Regional Conferences and a meeting of the Psi Upsilon
Foundation, Inc. in the early afternoon. Several hours of
free time found the delegates involved in a myriad of
activities �
exploring the sights of Vancouver, playing
golf, swimming, boating, and, for a few of the not-sohearty ones, catching up on some much needed sleep.
Alumni and undergraduates separated Friday evening,
each to "do their own thing.
"
Alumni were treated to an
elegant cocktail party at the Royal Vancouver Yacht Club,
replete with all manner of hors d'oeuvres and libations,
after which small groups formed to explore some of Van
couver's best attractions. Meanwhile the undergraduates
journeyed to the Sam Lock Restaurant in the heart of
Vancouver's Chinatown to feast on a scrumptious
Chinese meal before returning to the House for a party
featuring the band "Alcatraz."
Saturday morning's business session, entitled "Psi Up
silon �
Looking Down the Road," was a discussion on the
future direction of the Fraternity. Expertly led by Henry
B. Poor, Gamma '39, it enUghtened all present on the
ambitious plans in prospect for Psi Upsilon.
After luncheon the final standing committee meetings
and general meeting were held. On this last day of de
liberations, much intense thinking and debating were
done as the final legislation for the 138th Convention was
enacted. Some of the topics for consideration were an
appropriate commemoration of Psi Upsilon's One Hun
dred and Fiftieth Anniversary, long-range objectives and
programs envisioned in the Sesquicentennial Fund's
statement of purpose, total efimination of hazing in all its
manifestations, drug abuse, and undergraduate attrition.
Among the resolutions passed were the following:
1) The Lambda Chapter at Columbia University to host
the 139th Convention in 1982.
2) The Zeta Chapter at Dartmouth College to receive
the Psi Upsilon Award for Academic Distinction.
3) The Chi Chapter congratulated for earning the
approval ofthe Cornell University administration to reoccupy its Chapter House after a two-year hiatus.
4) The Zeta Tau Chapter at Tufts University welcomed
as the thirty-sixth Chapter to be chartered by Psi Upsilon
Fraternity.
5) Undergraduate dues raised to a one-time $70 mem
bership fee and a $40 tax for each year thereafter.
6) William H. Ducker, Phi '44 re-elected to a threeyear term on the Executive Council; Charles M. Hall, Nu
Alpha '71 and Stanton F. Weissenborn, Chi '49 re-elected
to five-year terms; and J. Laurence Costin, Jr. , Omega '63
elected to a three-year term.
7) Daniel J. Griffith, Chi Delta '83; John T. Kaplan,
Zeta '82; John R. Roberts, Epsilon Nu '82; and Peter
G. M. Wadsworth, Nu '82 elected undergraduate mem
bers of the Executive Council for one-year terms; and
Kenneth S. Ball, Eta '82; David W. Johns, II, Theta '82;
Stephen W. C. Rowell, Zeta Zeta '83; and D. John Walden, Xi '82 elected alternate undergraduate members for
one year terms.
Saturday evening's festivities came as a welcome re
spite after the long day of strenuous meetings. The Ex
ecutive Council hosted a delightful cocktail party at the
Graduate Student Centre, after which a sumptuous Con
vention banquet was served. Joseph W. Bishop, Zeta
Zeta '29, retired Brigadier General and charter member
of Alpha Kappa Alpha, the forerunner of the Zeta Zeta
Chapter, served as the principal speaker of the evening
and gave an entertaining account of the history of his
Chapter. Camaraderie abounded on this special night as
the good ol' Psi U songs were sung with gusto by all in
attendance. The spirit of brotherhood was never stronger
than when the assembled group finked hands, forming a
huge circle, and sang the Shrine Song . It was a fitting end
to a most memorable four days.
So many brothers contributed to the success of this
Convention that it would be impossible to name them all
here. But a special few should be mentioned. Ted Jef
ferys, Zeta Zeta '52, General Convention Chairman, and
Greg Wilson, Zeta Zeta '81, Undergraduate Convention
Chairman, deserve kudos for their months ofpreparation
which culminated in a smoothly run Convention. Strong
assists should go to all the undergraduates ofthe Zeta Zeta
Chapter and the energetic Convention committee, con
sisting of: James A. Clarke '54, Robert E. Fades '62,
Calvin B. Easter '56, A. Robert Hager '29, James A.
Maclnnes '50, David S. McDiarmid '64, John G. Preston
'55, William H. Preston '52, and A. Kenneth Thompson
'47, all members of the Zeta Zeta Chapter.
Sunday morning marked departure time for most ofthe
delegates. It was a weary but happy group that boarded
the planes, trains, and buses leaving from Vancouver for
the long trek home. The renewed brotherly spirit and
enthusiasm for Psi U with which they left bore testimon>
to the fact that the 138th Convention will be remembered
and reminisced about for a long time.

Thirty-Sixth Charter Granted to the
Zeta Tau Chapter at Tufts University
On Friday, April 24, 1981, twentythree members of the Tufts Provisional
Chapter were initiated into the ranks of
Psi Upsilon. The installation of the Zeta
Tau Chapter at Tufts University in Medford, Massachusetts represents one more
auspicious event in the annals of our
Fraternity. It is our first Chapter founded
in New England in more than a century,
our twenty-ninth active Chapter in the
United States and Canada, and our thirtysixth Chapter in the one hundred and
forty-eight years of Psi Upsilon's distin
guished history.
The formal installation ceremony, held
at the Sheraton Lexington Motor Inn,
was presided over by J. Russell McShane,
Delta '32, President of the Executive
Council. David A. B. Brown, Epsilon Phi
'66, President of the Zeta Tau Alumni
Association, served as master of cere
monies at the banquet which followed,
with Dean Bruce Reitman of Tufts Uni
versity and Hugh M. Walsh, Zeta Tau
'82, President of the new Chapter, de
livering appropriate remarks. Letters of
greeting and gifts from various Chapters,
alumni associations, and Executive
Council members were presented by
Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39, Executive
Vice President.
Interest in establishing a Chapter at
Tufts was first learned of through a tele
phone call on November 15, 1978 from a
freshman whose grandfather is a member
of the Tau, his father a member of the
Zeta, and his sister a member of the Iota.
Following an immediate visit by Michael
L. Huffman, Zeta '77, our Field Director
at the time, seven freshmen formally re
quested consideration six days later and
were pledged as members ofa Provisional
Chapter on December 5, 1978 by JeSrey
N. Colt, Zeta '76, David C. Hodgson,
Zeta '78, and John D. Macomber, Zeta
'77.
Tufts University is a strong liberal arts
institution, coeducational in enrollment,
with a number of well knovwi graduate
schools and eight active fraternities. On
Februar>' 6, 1979 the Provisional Chapter
was recognized officially as a campus
organization by the University's Commit
tee on Student Life. Psi Upsilon alumni
in the Boston area were invited to be
come in\olved, and at the second meet
ing of those interested, on.\priI 16, 1979,
David A. B. Brown, Epsilon Phi '66 was
elected President of the fledgling alumni
association, with John C. Brogan, Epsilon
Nu '55, John D. Macomber, Zeta '77, and
Eric A. Simonsen, Eta '67 accepting the
offices of Vice President, Secretary, and
Treasurer respectively.
By the fall of 1979, largely through the
efforts of Brother Huffman, an unfur
nished house was rented at 14 Whitfield
Road, virtually adjacent to the campus
and in the same area with other fraternity
houses. Many of the furnishings were
donated by interested alumni. The efforts
of the Provisional Chapter then were de
voted to meeting the recommended
guidelines adopted at the Fraternity's
135th Convention.
In the spring of 1981, having achieved a
membership of twenty-three and having
met the required guidelines, they pre
sented their formal petition and received
unanimous acceptance. They proposed
that the new Chapter be designated "Zeta
Tau" �

Psi Upsilon Mourns the Death of
Joseph A. Esquirol, Delta 17
Psi Upsilon has lost one of its most
dedicated brothers. Joseph A. Esquirol,
Delta '17, passed away September 20,
1981 at the Henry Perkins Adult Home in
Riverhead, Long Island at the age of
eighty-three.
Brother Esquirol attended his last Psi
Upsilon Convention in August, traveling
across the continent to Vancouver, Brit
ish Columbia. He had not missed a Con
vention in years. While there he suffered
a severe head wound when he fell on a
flight of stone steps. Hospitalized for two
days, he was allowed to return home, but
he never fully recovered.
Joe Esquirol gave himself completely
to whatever he undertook. As a young
attorney he opened a family law firm with
his younger brother, the late John H.
Esquirol, Delta '20, who some years
afterwards entered the ministry and be
came the Episcopal Bishop of Connecti
cut. Joe went on to become a distin
guished senator in the State of New York.
Following the death ofhis devoted wife
some years ago and his retirement from
active law practice. Brother Esquirol's
lifelong interest in his Fraternity became
his highest priority. Perhaps he is best
known among alumni and undergraduJoseph A. Esquirol
Delta 17
ates as Editor of the Diamond from 1974
until his death.
Prolific in his writing and energetic
beyond description, he beheved that the
distinguished careers of past alumni
could stimulate the efforts of younger
generations to new heights. His concept
of the quarterly publication was as a moti
vating force for what he firmly held to be
the finest fraternity of all.
Joe Esquirol's contributions to Psi Up
silon extended in many directions. He
had been a member of the Executive
Council since 1974 and an honorary
director of the Foundation since 1972.
Many years as secretary of the Delta Cor
poration were capped by two years as
president. For more than two decades he
edited the Delta Diamond, the Chapter's
newsletter.
Yet all these counted far less with him
than the joy of attending Delta Chapter
meetings regularly and serving as a coun
selor and friend to undergraduate
brothers. Just last May Joe was honored
by the Delta Chapter for "a lifetime of
dedication and devotion to the ideals and
traditions of our loved Psi Upsilon."
Beloved by all who knew him. Brother
Esquirol will be sorely missed. He is sur
vived by one son. Judge Joseph A. Es
quirol, Jr. Interment was in Cypress Hills
Cemetery in Brooklyn, New York.

The Wall Street Journal and
Reality Testing
The Wall Street Journal recently ran a
front page article entitled "Summer In
ternships Receive High Marks From Col
lege Students." Much of the article was
summed up by one student who stated,
"I've gotten the other side of what they
tell you in school ... all they can really
deal with in (the classroom) is theory."
The student was correct in his assess
ment of the role of the typical college or
university. Further, with many colleges
and universities compelled by rising costs
to cut back or restrict programs, under
graduates often find even less opportu
nity today for practical application in their
college experience.
Psi Upsilon, however, provides a chan
nel for filling this need. Indeed a major
role of the Fraternity always has been
"Reality Testing." We define "Reality
Testing" as the face-to-face experiences
in leadership, commitment, service, and
sociability, and running a business.
Fraternities do not deal extensively in
theory. Our undergraduate members
must deal with the day-to-day problems
of:
Selhng �

1949
The 1980-81 academic year was both
disappointing and rewarding for the
brothers of the Epsilon Omega. Starting
with fifteen empty room spaces and a
period of low House morale, the fall and
winter officers had a difficult time manag
ing not only House funds but also regular
Chapter affairs. In addition to these prob
lems, a traditional pledge activity re
sulted in a twelve-month University
probation, due to irresponsibility of the
brothers. Consequently the House faced
a rather substantial debt, as well as
strained relations with the Northwestern
University administration.
The newly elected spring officers,
along with the brothers, were deter
mined to start the House moving in a
different direction. The first obstacle to
avoid was the financial difficulty which
loomed before the Chapter. Having re
viewed the spring quarter financial fig
ures, we are proud to announce that the
Chapter finished the quarter in the black
for the first time in three years. Accom
panying the swing in financial trend was
an
equally important movement within
the House toward a more spirited atti
tude.
Examples of our improved morale
were illustrated in some of our activities
auring the spring quarter. One such
event was the Northwestern University
alumni phonathon. Our highly motivated
group raised over $2,500 for the Alumni
Association, and we are
hoping to im
prove on that performance this fall. Two
other activities worth mentioning are the
spring formal and the annual Psi UpsilonAlpha Tau Omega-Delta Gamma party.
Both were tremendous successes and can
be attributed directly to the efforts of our
social chairman and the support of the
brothers.
Other excellent accomplishments were
rung up during the year by the brothers
on the playing field. Our football team
finished fourth in the intramural tourna
ment, after an astonishing upset of top
ranked A.T.O. In addition our coed
swimming team won its fourth straight
intramural championship. Further many
brothers competed at the varsity level. Of
this group one brother was honored as an
All-Big-Ten selection in tennis, and many
others were regular starters in baseball,
lacrosse, soccer, and tennis.
One reason for whatever successes we
achieved both on and off the field was the
constant support offered by the graduat
ing class. Of that group three have de
cided to pursue a law degree, three hope
fully will become doctors, and two are
enrolled in graduate business schools.
Joining this distinguished company are
two working with I.B.M. and two in the
television industry.
The loss of such a good group of seniors
is painful for the Chapter, but the incom
ing delegation of twenty-one pledges has
shown us that they can fill their shoes
effectively. Not only have they proven to
be scholars, but they have excelled in
athletics and have shown themselves to
be fine young men.
With these new additions we look to
ward a fall which appears to be very
promising. For the first time in two years
the brothers of the Epsilon Omega return
to a full House. Obviously this helps our
financial situation, and the psychological
boost of a full House is immeasurable.
Furthermore the officers for this term are
competent, responsible young men, and
the brothers are eager to follow their
leadership.
Evan A . Williams '82
President

Upsilon, the Chi Delta is the newest
fraternity on the Duke University cam
pus. With brothers hailing from Mas
sachusetts to Wisconsin, the Chi Delta is

the academic year with twenty brothers,

survive. Small in number, we face prob
lems which are peculiar to groups of that
size. We require the active participation
of each brother in every phase of our
fraternal life. In looking at our year's per
formance, it appears evident that we do
have this teamwork.

pledges, a clear reflection of the hard
work done by the whole brotherhood. In
honor of our new brothers we held our
first pledge formal, with each brother
purchasing glasses to commemorate the
affair. It was a splendid CM-ning, from the
shrimp cocktail and chocolate mousse to
the fine band which played after the
meal, to the introduction of the newest
links in the Psi Upsilon chain.

vidual ability, and an eagerness to partici
pate in all fields of endeavor. This award

ber of the Chi Delta, because each

ious to the needs of our less fortunate

breaks. Their help does not go unheeded,

ings.

splendor that is Psi Upsilon.

them.
